(a) M/s Thermax Ltd.-the appellant-Company, is a Public
Limited Company having its registered office at Chinchwad, Pune and is engaged in the field of
energy and environment management. Mr. K.M. 260062 for designing and manufacturing two numbers of stationary L.P.G. Storage Tanks
and Order Nos. 260063 and 260064 were for the supply of consumables and other accessories to
the said Tanks. 1 and in their opinion even though they have not made any static bullets and have made quite a few
mobile L.P.G. Tanks, however, they were capable of manufacturing the same, but needed design
help. 1 was provided with the necessary steel of the technical
specification. 1 had not ordered for consumables and no rectification and
drawings had been carried out. 1 was not
interested in executing the assignment. 1 agreed to complete the job by all means by
22.09.1995. 1 failed to carry out the work as per the Schedule, the
effective from 26.05.1995 i.e., from the date when the order was placed. 1 filed a complaint with the Crime Branch, Pune alleging that
they had carried out several fabrication job works for the appellant-Company and huge amount of
Rs. 91,95,054/- was outstanding till date despite several requests.

12 of 2002 and by order dated 30.05.2002,
the Judicial Magistrate issued a direction under Section 156(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure,
1973 (in short `the Code') and referred the same to Crime Branch, Pune, Respondent No. The High Court, vide order dated 18.10.2006, issued rule and interim relief by directing the
Assistant Commissioner of Police, Crime Branch-II, Pune city to produce the documents within six
weeks in the Court of Judicial Magistrate, Pimpri. The Company issued material after receipt of pay order, vide excise gate Pass No. The
complainant requested the accused to take the scrap material back and issue genuine material. 9) Now, we have to find out whether the ingredients of Sections 405, 420 read with Section 34 have
been made out from the complaint and whether the Magistrate is justified in calling for a report
under Section 156(3) of the Code from the Crime Branch, Pune. Simultaneously, we have to see
whether the High Court is justified in confirming the action of the Magistrate and failed to exercise
its power and jurisdiction under Section 482 of the Code. A legal notice was issued to the appellant therein on 11.07.1996 calling upon
him to execute the sale deed in respect of the premises in question. A charge-sheet was filed on 04.08.2000 by the police against the
the alleged offence under Section 190(1)(b) of the Code and issued summons to the
accused-appellant therein. Despite this, the Magistrate issued process against Accused Nos. In that proceeding, the appellant-Company moved an
application under Section 93 of the Code to issue a search warrant to seize the property in dispute
and also to hand over these items to the complainant. The Magistrate took cognizance of the alleged
complaint and issued summons to the respondents and passed an order on the application filed
under Section 93 of the Code to have a search at the premises of the respondents and to take
possession of the properties involved in the case. The learned Single Judge was pleased to quash the entire proceedings and
directed the appellant-Company to return all the properties seized by the police pursuant to the
warrant issued by the Magistrate.

2007 before the High Court. The High Court, vide order dated 11.01.2008, dismissed the writ
petition as misconceived on the ground that the Magistrate has adhered to the directions and has
given reasons for coming to his conclusion. 12 of 2002 and the impugned order of the
High Court dated 11.01.2008, at the outset, submitted that the courts below ought to
have considered that the dispute arose out of a contract and a constituted remedy is
only before a civil court. He further
submitted that the High Court ought to have intervened and quashed the same. According to him,
the complaint and the allegations made therein do not disclose any offence and, therefore, the
direction under Section 156(3) of the Code is untenable. 1/complainant submitted that interference by the court at the stage of passing orders under Section
156 (3) of the Code is not warranted. He further pointed out that the accused has no right to address
at this stage and the High Court is right in refusing to entertain the petition filed under Section 482
of the Code. Therefore, the complainant requested the Accused for the supply of material for the said order and
to debit the material cost from the final bill. Therefore, complainant paid Rs. Thus, the accused
have cheated the complainant and there by caused wrongful loss to the complainant.
